executive_summary: The central thread running through today's content is the contested status of power, legitimacy, and who gets to define the rules of major institutions — from politics and law to sports and gender itself. The Atlantic's deep investigation into masculinism exposes it as a coordinated ideological project aimed at dismantling hard-won institutional equality for women, framing reaction as reform and misogyny as grievance. This connects directly to Foreign Affairs' examination of Orbán's fall and Europe's realignment, where authoritarian actors who built power by weaponizing cultural resentment are now facing structural resistance from the institutions they sought to undermine. Even in the sports sphere, The Athletic's coverage of WNBA officiating problems and college football's playoff expansion reflects the same underlying tension: who controls the frameworks that govern competition, and whether those frameworks serve the many or entrench the powerful. Taken together, today's content tells a story about a global inflection point in which legacy power structures are being challenged from multiple directions simultaneously — and the outcome of those contests will define the next decade of political, cultural, and institutional life.

items.blurb: Forty-eight minutes and 42 seconds. Forty-one points. Twenty-four rebounds. Three assists. Three blocks. One massive 28-foot 3-pointer. That was Victor Wembanyama's stat line from the Spurs' 122-115 double-overtime victory in Game 1 of the Western Conference finals last night. Since blocked shots started being recorded in the 1973-74 season, only three players have put up 40 points, 24 boards and three blocks in a playoff game. Hakeem Olajuwon did it twice in 1987 and 1988. Shaquille O'Neal did it in 2000. Now Wemby.

newsletters.title: Here’s why Elon Musk lost his suit against OpenAI

items.headline: Here's why Elon Musk lost his suit against OpenAI
items.blurb:
Elon Musk has lost his lawsuit against OpenAI, which centered on whether the company breached its founding contract as a nonprofit. A jury found that he sued too late, meaning his claims are barred by statutes of limitations. But the verdict didn't judge if OpenAI violated its nonprofit mission—only whether Musk brought the case in time.

The dispute hinged on when OpenAI began shifting toward a for-profit structure. The company argued that signs of a shift were visible as early as 2017, while Musk said he only discovered the change in 2022.

items.headline: Inside Anduril and Meta's quest to make smart glasses for warfare
items.blurb:
The defense-tech company Anduril has shared new details about the augmented-reality headset for the military it's prototyping with Meta, including a vision for ordering drone strikes via eye-tracking and voice commands.

Quay Barnett, who leads the effort at Anduril following a career in the Army's Special Operations Command, says he aims to optimize "the human as a weapons system."

items.headline: What to expect at Google I/O this week
items.blurb:
When Google opens its doors today for its annual developer conference, I/O, it will do so as a clear third place in the foundation model race.

A foundation model's reputation these days rests largely on its coding capabilities, and for months Google's coding tools have been outgunned by Anthropic's Claude Code and OpenAI's Codex. But the company still shapes the cutting edge in areas such as AI for science. At I/O this week, it will try to prove it can compete on both fronts.

items.headline: Can AI learn to understand the world?
items.blurb:
As the limits of LLMs become clearer, researchers are developing a new kind of AI designed to understand the physical environment: world models.

Recent developments from Google DeepMind, Fei-Fei Li's World Labs, and Yann LeCun's new startup have pushed these systems to the forefront of AI. At an upcoming virtual event, MIT Technology Review will examine the progress—and what comes next.

longform.title: Why I don’t buy masculinism
longform.thesis: Masculinism — a coordinated right-wing movement seeking to reverse feminist gains including women's suffrage and workplace equality — represents not a response to genuine male suffering but a virulent, politically motivated misogyny that has become the central ideological adhesive of the American right.
longform.context: The piece serves as an author's note introducing Helen Lewis's June 2026 Atlantic cover story, prompted by the visible rise of self-described masculinist thinkers gaining mainstream political proximity, including figures connected to Pete Hegseth and the Trump movement.
arguments: Feminism's success — not its failure — explains the ferocity of masculinist backlash: Lewis argues that because women have made 'simply extraordinary' gains since 1857, the movement to reverse those gains is explicitly reactive, with masculinists openly calling for repealing the Nineteenth Amendment, instituting a 'family wage,' and reversing the 'great feminization' of professional life.

Masculinism is populated by ideologically distinct but mutually reinforcing figures — Douglas Wilson (theological patriarchalism tied to Hegseth's denomination), Raw Egg Nationalist (pseudoscientific testosterone politics linking liberalism to low T), and Helen Andrews (civilizational anti-feminism) — whose convergence suggests an organized intellectual ecosystem, not fringe commentary.

The masculinist movement strategically targets empathy as a political weapon, framing it as 'a dangerous, feminine softness toward immigrants and criminals,' which Lewis identifies as the connective tissue between gender reaction and broader right-wing authoritarian politics.

Lewis draws a critical analytical distinction: she accepts that 'some men and boys are struggling in ways that don't get enough attention' (citing male problem gambling rates) but rejects the masculinist causation that feminism produced this suffering — refusing to conflate legitimate male distress with the political program built on top of it.
longform.significance: The piece matters because it frames masculinism not as a cultural curiosity but as 'the single most important force holding together the American right,' elevating it from internet subculture to a structural political analysis. It arrives at a moment when masculinist figures hold or influence federal office, making the ideological genealogy Lewis traces directly relevant to policy. By separating real male disadvantage from masculinist exploitation of that disadvantage, the piece also challenges both dismissive liberal responses and credulous conservative ones.
questions_raised: If masculinism functions as ideological glue for the right, what — if anything — constitutes a politically viable counter-movement that addresses genuine male struggles without conceding the masculinists' causal framework blaming feminism?

The author notes she was 'a little daunted' by separating 'well-evidenced facts from lazy stereotypes' in gender discourse — the newsletter form leaves unresolved how rigorously the full piece adjudicates which masculinist empirical claims (e.g., on male educational decline) have merit versus which are fabricated grievance.
